projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Fred See was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: We are at the Gaylord Opryland Resort and Convention Center in Nashville, Tennessee, at the National Court Reporter's Foundation's VHP day. Today is Friday, August 9th, 2013. My name is Ann Banta, and I'm here to interview Fred See. Mr. See, was born on what day? When were you born?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Oh, January 8, 1941.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: All right. He served in the Army, was it?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Correct.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: From what date to what date?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: September--I'm sorry, August 31st until 1976 sometime.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: Okay. August of what year, 1941?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Oh, August--no, no.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: No, you were born in 1941. I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Yes. In 1963.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: That was when I was born. Okay. This interview is being conducted for the Veterans History Project at the Library of Congress. I'm going to ask you a series of questions to try and capture your experience in the United States military. Okay. These are going to be the biographical details. Tell me a bit about your family, where you grew up.

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Okay. I grew up on a farm in Iowa, between Iowa City and Cedar Rapids, Iowa, and went to a one-room country schoolhouse from kindergarten through seventh grade. I was the only one in my class. And then I went to a small high school--middle school and high school, Solon, Iowa, and then I went to college at Iowa State University, went through ROTC. Was in Pershing rifles and drill teams and graduated in August 1963.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: All right. I see that you were drafted, enlisted in the Army. When you entered the military, how long had the war been going on or was there a war going on?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: No, I don't think there was a war going on. I went to officers basic at Fort Sill, Oklahoma, and then I went to Airborne School at Fort Benning, Georgia, and completed that. And then I went--my wife and I went to Germany, and I was--the first year and a half I was an advisor with special weapons to the Belgian Army, two battalions. Then I transferred--I was transferred to the Second Armored Cavalry. I was a battery commander for artillery battery with the Second Armored Cavalry. They patrolled the Czech border, and we went out there sometimes. And that's when they were communist, and then from there I went to Vietnam. And when I arrived in Vietnam, I was a fire direction officer for field artillery and then became the battalion S2, which is intelligence officer, and some of the special duties I had I was an air observer and also a military lawyer without any previous law experience. They gave me a book and said, read this and you will be a lawyer. So that's what I did.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: Oh, my.

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: That was a secondary. Because out in the jungle where I was if there was a court martial case, the aviator and I, we flew to where we were supposed to be, and I looked for the enemy along the way. And then we had the court martial, and then we would fly back in combat area again. I learned how to land the plane because the aviator said, if he got wounded and blacked out, he wanted to make sure I could land it properly without crashing it. And so I learned how to land the airplane, but I never learned how to takeoff.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: So you're sort of a pilot too, a little bit.

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Well, a little bit, yes.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: My goodness. Okay. So--and then you also said you served in Desert Storm?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Correct. I--when I got out of the Army in 1969, I stayed in the Army Reserve and then moved to Tennessee and--with Oscar Mayer and joined an Army Reserve unit here in Nashville. It was a military police prisoner of war camp. So I became a--I was the assistant 3, S3 operations officer. Then I became the commander for the prisoner of war camp and then later on commander of a military police prisoner of war detachment.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: Oh, my goodness. So you--to be clear you were not drafted. You were enlisted.

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Well, I took ROTC in college, and I was--when I graduated, I got the commission of a regular Army officer, similar to--to a certain extent like West Point, regular Army instead of Reserve, and so I had years of a commitment because they--my junior and senior year they paid for my tuition. So I wanted to fulfill that commitment, and I enjoyed it at the time.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: Okay. At the moment after your--it says drafted or enlisted but--

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: How did you feel?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Oh, I felt great. It was--I enjoyed the military, and I was gung-ho, started Ranger School after Airborne. However, after the second week when we were to go to the Florida phase, one of the students got--he drowned, and so they put a hold on the Rangers, and they called me in and said, would you--you are scheduled to go to Europe for three years. Would you--do you still want to go to Europe, or if you want to finish Ranger school, we will cancel the European assignment, and then when you graduate from Ranger School, we will send you to Korea? And I had just been married for about, oh, a few months, so I decided that my wife and I would go to Europe. So that's what happened.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: That sounds neat. How did your parents feel about you serving?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Oh, they thought it was great. They were very proud. As a matter of fact, my whole community was proud. Even after--through and after Vietnam. They sent me a lot of packages. When I came back, they were all, you know, glad to see me, and they were very complimentary.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: That's great. Did you have other family members in the war?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Yes, I did. Well, not that war. Vietnam I don't believe I had any other family members in that war. In Desert Storm I did. And I had a cousin that was in the same major unit that I was in, and it was funny because I was a lieutenant colonel and I commanded seven units in Desert Storm and was a senior liaison officer to the Saudi Arabians from my general in the 800th Military Police Brigade. So I found out my cousin came over, he was in the National Guard in Iowa. So I got a letter from my aunt saying that he was over there and she was worried about him. So I went down to his unit and said, I need a driver. You know, I asked him if he would like to be my driver. And he said, no. He wanted to stay with his unit. And I said, fine, that's--I thought that is what you would say. And I said, but I just wanted to let you know that I'm here. And so anyway I called his--I called his--not I called. I wrote his mother and said that he is in my unit, and I will watch over him. So it made her feel good.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: That's a neat story. All right. Our next topic is going to be early days of service. And what was training camp like?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Oh, training camp, that was officers basic, and it was a lot of fun. We met other officers and their wives and family, and we got along very well and went on picnics and--out in the mountains of--Wichita Mountains in Oklahoma. And we had a--we had a very good time, and we went through a lot. I remember we were all in a classroom when President Kennedy was assassinated, and so class was cut short that day. But we all felt bad about that, but we all--we were just like a big family.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: And so where did you attend training camp?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: At Fort Sill, Oklahoma.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: All right. Now, what were your specific duties that you were being trained for?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Field artillery. Well, command and also operation of artillery, whether you were a forward observer, battery XO, executive officer, worked in the fire direction center, and basically anything that we could--that would come along. Leadership basically, mainly.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: All right. Where were you stationed during your service?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Okay. I was stationed at Fort Sill, of course, at the beginning for officers basic. Then I went to Fort Benning for Airborne. Then I went to Cologne, Germany, got my first unit. And that was with the--as an advisor to the Belgian artillery. I had two battalions. I was the special weapons advisor to them. And then from there transferred to Hamburg, Germany, and that's when I was with the Second Armored Cavalry howitzer battery. And I was--started out as executive officer and then became battery commander. Then I went to Vietnam and started out there as a battalion fire direction officer and then was given the position of battalion S2, which is intelligence officer. And that's when I had the other items that I--other additional duties. Then after Vietnam, came back to Fort Sill and was an instructor for--trying to think--sensory equipment division from the target acquisition department, and that was an instructor and then the commander or the head of the sensory equipment division made me his executive officer. And it was interesting, this is a story, the target acquisition department built a new building, and my commander came in and said, see if you can come up with a good name for this building. It was--so I said, okay. So I thought how am I going to get my name on that building? And then I remembered that Fort Sill, Oklahoma, there was a--one of the early scouts for the Calvary, his name was I-See, which was spelled S-E-E, dash O. So I wrote up the application for the name of the building, and I said, I-See-O was an American Indian and he was the first target--one of the first target acquisition positions in the United States Army. And so this is--building is target acquisition, so I recommend that we name it I-SEE-O, and not only that but it would be good--good communication and relationship with the American Indians in Oklahoma. So that's what they named the building.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: Very clever.

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Okay. Then after that I went into the Army Reserve and came to Nashville, and then I got called up again for Desert Storm. So then I went over with the military police prisoner of war unit from Nashville to Saudi Arabia, and the general from the 800th Military Police Brigade assigned me as the commander of seven military police small units and then also as chief liaison officer with the Saudi Arabians during Desert Storm.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: And what was day-to-day life like? What were your responsibilities?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Oh, I had a lot of responsibilities. Day-to-day life was busy. I enjoyed it. I didn't have a lot of free time. I just enjoyed my work and working with other people, and I just kept busy. Didn't have any--very little spare time.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: How did the locals receive you where you were stationed?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Well, in Fort Sill locals were very good. Same thing here in the United States everywhere. Germany was great because my ancestors came from Germany, and so I could speak a little German. And working with the Belgians I tried to learn French because that's what a lot of them spoke, other than English, and I got along very well with them. We had parties together. Then in Vietnam, I got--I met a lot--quite a few Vietnamese nationals, and we had, you know, got along with them. And then Saudi Arabia was even--was really fantastic because I tried to learn the Arabic language, and I worked very closely with the Saudis and helped them set up their prisoner of war camps, helped them run their camps according to the Geneva Convention. And matter of fact, I got comments made to my general that they considered me one of their people. So I--that was quite a compliment so--and I enjoyed working with them as well.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: Were you constantly waiting for the call to go into combat?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: No, I--no. I was--in Europe we patrolled the Czech border when they were--and also with the Belgian Army we had plans in case an emergency came up. So, you know, we were always ready. Vietnam combat was just like Russian roulette, you never know, you know, if you were going to make it through the day. I was in the--up along the Cambodian border in the jungle. And we got--during the Tet Offensive we got hit almost every night, so it was pretty interesting. I got--I was in a helicopter once that I think we--it appeared that a sniper hit it, and so we had to crash land in the jungle. We didn't crash land real hard because we could auto rotate. We had enough power, and that was kind of scary. I led--I was told to go check out this one area in the jungle to see if I could teach the people--started out to teach the people to grow rice because I was replacing a captain from Louisiana. And I told the commander, I don't know how to--I don't know how to grow rice. And he said, well, where are you from? And I said, Iowa. He said, what do you crow there? I said, corn. He said, the kind you eat? And I said, yes, the kind you eat or the kind that you give to livestock. So he said, well, go see if you can teach them how to grow corn because he wanted to have them process it and make money, this little village Nuc Van. So I told my sergeant--I was in the fire direction center at the time in Vietnam. I told him, I said, tomorrow I want my Jeep with two radios with two radio operators and three or more other Jeeps with machine guns on them, and we are going to go out, and I want volunteers. I don't want to make anybody go out there. Well, the next morning we had all kinds of volunteers. I had three other Jeeps with machine guns so we drove off, and we arrived at the clearing. He showed me on the--the commander showed me the map on where the clearing was where he wanted me to see if they could grow corn. So I told the sergeant, I said, okay. When we pulled up, I said, I want the Jeep with the two radios sitting right here. I want the radio operators right there next to the radio in case we run into problems to call for help. I want one machine gun pointing to my left at the jungle in case the enemy was in there. I want another machine gun pointing to my right, and there was people working in a rice paddy, and I thought why did he want the other captain to teach them how to grow rice when they already knew how to grow rice. But anyway, they were working in the rice paddy. And I wanted the third machine gun to cover us as we walked in the open area in case there were enemy in spider holes pop up and shoot us. So I said, the rest of you men follow me. So we were walking out single file, and I looked back and they were three meters apart with their rifles at the ready, and I thought this is--they really know what they're doing. And I was keeping my eye on the people working in the rise paddies because I didn't know--I had only been there for about two or three weeks, and I didn't know if they were friendly or what. Pretty soon they stopped working and stood up and was watching us. And then later on one man waved his arms and was yelling at us in Vietnamese. So I put up my hand, and I said, halt. And I said, can anybody speak Vietnamese? Nobody could speak Vietnamese because the interpreter had gone out with another part of the unit that morning. So I thought, well, when I was with the Belgians in Europe, I learned to speak a little French, and this was a colony, Vietnam was a colony of France, maybe somebody over there can speak French. So I yelled at him in French, what is the problem? And he answered me in French you walked in the middle of a mine field. So then I was concerned that my--if I told my troops--they were looking at me because they couldn't understand French, and they were looking at me as if to say what did he say? And I didn't want them to panic and run. So I yelled at them basically I don't want anybody to do anything. Just standstill and listen to me and do what I tell you exactly. Don't do anything other than what I tell you. And I said, I will get you out of here if you listen and follow my orders. They just told me that we are in the middle of a mine field. I looked--I was looking over my shoulder and their faces just became pale. And I said, everybody look on the ground, you will see our footprints. Carefully turn around and step in the same footprints, and we can get out. And that's what we did. Now, I followed them, and they were very careful, and we got out without anybody getting hurt. And then a couple of weeks later I got the--word came down through channels that they wanted the Vietnamese and the higher headquarters asked if I would go out and remove the mines. And I said, well, okay, give me the diagram where the mines are located because you're supposed to do that. And they said, we don't have it. The Vietnamese officer that put the mines in, he was a lieutenant, he's got it all up in his head where he put it. I said, fine, then he can get the mines out. And then two days later he blew himself up, so we were fortunate that we didn't do that.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: You mentioned spider holes, what are spider holes?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Well, okay--that's--I remember in the movies, you know, with--the enemy is under the ground and they got--they call them spider holes. They got camouflage on top of the holes, and then when you get close, they pop up and shoot.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: Okay. All right. How were you able to stay in touch with home while you were abroad?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Oh, well, that was all by mail, snail mail. And when I was in Desert Storm, I could call a couple of times. I did make two phone calls. Now, one was when my father-in-law passed away, I called my wife, and she said, are you sure you're over in Saudi Arabia? And I said, yes. She said, well, because we went to--I called the home office of your--of the unit, and they said that they didn't know where you were. So I said, well, here I am. So, yeah, that's--other than that, it was snail mail.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: What were some of your off-duty recreational pursuits?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Over in Europe I coached flag football and I coached basketball. Flag football I didn't play because the men would call me sir, and I knew if I played flag football instead of getting the flag, the opposing team would tackle me so--because they knew I was an officer, so I just coached them. And then basketball I just coached our local team played against the Germans. Other than that, recreation was just--I really didn't have that much. My recreation was doing my job.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: You didn't do any sightseeing or--

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Oh, well, in Europe my wife and I--her grandmother came over, and we drove around to the other--but in Saudi Arabia and Vietnam, no. That was--I was all over any way so I did a lot of sightseeing with my subordinate units and flying in the aircraft. One day we were--I was--we were flying, and like I said, we got--something happened to the engine, we don't know whether a sniper hit it or what. So when we landed hard--as we were landing, the aviator said--this was a helicopter--he said, I'm going to land right there, call in the grid coordinators because I always carried a map and I knew where we were to call in for artillery. So I called in and I said, mayday, mayday. I finally got to use that term like it should be used. And I told them that we have been--we lost power, we possibly have been hit, and we were going to land and I give them the grid coordinators. And they said, we should be there within 15, 20 minutes to get you out of there. Well, when we landed, we landed kind of hard and it was tall grass. And so the aviator and I, we was trying to decide what we were going to do. We had different options. We talked about--one option was staying in the helicopter so that when they came to get us out they could see us, but then the enemy could see us too. So that wasn't too good. The other one was to get out of the helicopter and walk away in case the enemy shot it with a grenade launcher or a bazooka or whatever. But we was afraid if we got out and walked in that tall grass, we might walk into the enemy because we knew the enemy was there somewhere. The other option, the third option was to crawl under neither the helicopter so that we could get the radio receiver out and be in contact in case they had trouble finding us. And then also they--when we see them, we could tell them, and then they would know that we were there. And so we did that. We sat underneath back to back, and we each had a rifle and a pistol so we had 360-degree observation and, of course, the grass it was kind of a little bit of wind and it would blow, and it would look like the enemy was coming through and you would tense up and get ready to pull the trigger and then it would go back. But it seemed like forever, but it was between 15 and 20 minutes before they came and got us out. So that was interesting.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: Wow, that 15 minutes must have seemed like a lifetime.

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: It did.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: What was it like as a relatively young man handling a weapon? Were you nervous?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Well, no. I grew up on a farm. I was familiar with weapons, rifles, pistols. When I--one of my additional duties was--in Vietnam was to work with the Special Forces, the Green Berets, and one night during the Tet Offensive one afternoon they called and said they wanted a staff officer to come to their Special Forces camp out in the jungle because they thought they would get--might get overrun that night, and they wanted a staff officer. Well, the commander wasn't going to go, and he wasn't going to send his XO. The S1 was admin, and he wasn't that familiar with artillery, calling in artillery, setting up defensive concentrations. The S3 was a major, and he was in charge of the operations and the fire direction center, so he wasn't going to go. And the S4 was back in Long Ben so that left me. So I went out to the Special Forces camp and that--they said, where is your rifle? And I said, well, I got my .45 pistol. And they said, well, no, if you're going to be with us, we're going to give you a rifle. So they gave me a Carbine--

sp.speaker: Sheryl G. Weatherford
sp.p: They gave you what?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: A carbine, C-A-R-B-I-N-E. It's a rifle, but it's not like an M-1 or an M-16. And then they said--okay. I went to the briefing because they wanted me to have a rifle. So I had two weapons, and they said, tonight if we get overrun, we are going to run through the jungle to this area here where there was a fork in the river, and it was about 15 kilometers--and eight kilometers is a mile. So we are going to run through the jungle tonight, and then we will stop at this--and then we will get extracted from there. We will call in helicopters. And I thought run through the jungle at night? I'm just going to grab one of their shirt tails and let them lead me through and--but as it turned out, I found out they really didn't need me. So they wanted to me to plan defensive concentrations. And these Special Forces, Green Beret guys, they knew how to do that. But I found out--I realized why they wanted me there was because we had eight howitzers in our battalion at the time, and there was ten Special Forces camps. So they wanted to make sure that if they had a staff officer, they got first priority. And that's the only reason they wanted me because they had everything set up.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: They're very clever too.

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Yes. There's a lot of clever people in the United States Army. That's why when people say, well, weren't you worried about your son or your grandsons, you know? I said, they're in the best Army in the world, you know, and we got a lot of smart people in our military.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: Best in the world. Yes. Were there any accidents involving handling those weapons with you or any of your friends?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Yes. I have a friend--I'm not going to mention his name--he was giving a class in Saudi Arabia on weapons, specialty pistols. When you go into an area, you're supposed to make sure that you take the ammunition out of your weapon and then just--that's number one. Check it and slide it back, make sure there's no ammunition in the weapon. Then you point it in a barrel full of sand and pull the trigger just to be safe. He was giving a class on this, and he was telling about it, and, of course, he pulled out his weapon, slid the--slid it back and said, see, there's--first of all, you check and make sure there's no weapon in the chamber. Then you point it. And he pointed it at the wall because it was inside the classroom, and he pulled the trigger and it went off. So you could see the bullet in the wall. So the people that were in there they drew a circle around, made a target out of it. So he never did live that down.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: That's funny. Did you ever get homesick while you were serving?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: No. No. Because they sent, you know, letters and never--not really. You know, I missed being home, but I never got really homesick.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: The war end and coming home. Were you on active duty when the war ended, which we have got two wars here so...

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Right. No, I wasn't on active duty when Vietnam ended--well, yes, I was. I was in Fort Sill, Oklahoma, as an instructor. Wait a minute, I got to think about that. No. No. I was not--I was in--off of active duty because I got out on June 1969. So the war was still going on, but I was in the Army Reserve. And then in Desert Storm I was on active duty when the war ended. We came home then afterwards.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: Were you awarded any medals?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Oh, yes. And I thought to--when I got here, I should have brought my DD214. But I had two bronze stars, one from each war, meritorious medal, a lot of--a couple of Army commendation medals, the Vietnamese cross of gallantry, the liberation of Kuwait and Saudi Arabian medal and some other medals and ribbons.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: Do you have them on display? Do you have a nice box that you hang on the wall?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: No. I'm thinking about doing that. But I have--because I go to a--I teach--substitute teach high schools and a lot of it is ROTC, JROTC, and I did teach ROTC at Vanderbilt one year and also Tennessee State but--so I have got my miniature medals to wear on my suit, and I--of course, I've got the medals for my uniform too, but I don't--didn't put them in a display case yet.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: Okay. My mom did that for my great uncle. So he appreciated it. What was the reception by family and the community like?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: It's always been great, even Vietnam. Community, the family when I came back, they were very appreciative of all the veterans and what we have done. And it was different than what--from what I hear from other people, and so I was very fortunate. Especially when we came back from Desert Storm, we flew into Fort Campbell. And they said, okay, what we are going to do, the first people off the plane will be Vietnam veterans who have fought in this war to give them a chance to get off first and--because families and everybody was out there, you know, yelling and greeting us. So that was pretty nice I thought for them to do that.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: How did you readjust to civilian life?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Well, since I stayed in the Army Reserve, I readjusted very well. The civilian life it--you know, the civilians are very nice. As a matter of fact when--before I went to Desert Storm, some of the secretaries at Oscar Mayer I was in management in the plant, and they said, aren't you concerned that you will get called up for Desert Storm? And I said, no, no. I said, it would have to really get bad if I got called up. And wouldn't you know it, a week later I got my orders to go. So that was funny.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: All right. Now, we move on to reflections. When you think back about being in the Armed Forces, is there one particular moment in time that stands out in your mind for any reason? For instance, a moment when you were the most scared, the happiest, the most proud to be an American serviceman?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Well, the most scared was leading the people in and out of the mine field. Secondly was when our air helicopter went down, and probably the Tet Offensive at night when they were trying to overrun us, you know, and we were shooting back. Those are the three most scared. Most proud is coming home, you know, and seeing how the people appreciated what we did. Was there anything else?

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: The happiest.

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Oh, the happiest, being back with my family.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: What is the most important life lesson you've learned from your military service?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Think and don't panic. And when I teach the students at high school and middle school, a lot of times they ask me, you know, to tell some stories and I--or what advice I might have. I said, always stop and think, never panic, think. You can think your way out of a lot of situations. But if you panic, you're going to get caught up in some situations that you have a difficult time getting out of. And tell them, you know, God gave you a brain to think with, so be sure you use it.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: Is there anything you would like to say to those who may read this account in the Library of Congress from the standpoint of a veteran who has served his country?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Well, yes. Always think about the people around you and the troops that are subordinate that look up for you for guidance. Another story happened, and this happened in Desert Storm. I got--received a letter--a call from a commander, one of my subordinate commanders, saying that his troops are supposed to go get inoculated, and they won't put what the inoculation is on their shot cards. And so they were a little concerned, and I said, okay, when are you supposed to go get your inoculations? He said, tomorrow afternoon at 1300, one o'clock. I said, I will be there. So I was there, and I went with his troops up to get inoculated, and I said, I will be the first one to be inoculated. However, here is my shot card, put what you're going to go to inoculate me with on my shot card. They said, we can't do that. And I said, why can't you? They said, because we were given orders not to do that. And I said, well, look, I have been in Vietnam and we were in Agent Orange, and I was in Agent Orange, and we thought, you know, the government wouldn't do anything to hurt us. So Agent Orange was just something that they sprayed to defoliate the trees, and then we found out afterwards that it wasn't--I mean, that it was to defoliate, but it also was a health hazard as well. So I'm not going to get inoculated until you put it on my shot card, and my men, whom I responsible for, are not going to get inoculated until you put it on their shot card. And they said, well, you will have to talk to our colonel. And I said, fine. When do you want to talk--when do you want me to talk to him? They said, well, I can set it up for later on this afternoon. I said, fine. Tell your colonel that I will be there to talk to him, but I'm going to bring a reporter with me. And that--later on that afternoon I got a call from the colonel said, okay, tomorrow morning we will give you inoculations, and we will put it on your shot card. So my troops were happy, you know, and they put what was on there. And it was--it was for--excuse me. It was anthrax. And I said, anthrax? I said, that's--I'm from Iowa, and there's a lot of people that raise sheep and, yes, anthrax is a disease. But I said, if you're inoculated for it, all you need to do in my opinion is to keep us there for another half hour or an hour to watch to make sure we don't--no one has a reaction. But I said, well--I said, why are you so concerned? They said, because people back in the United States, other than those in the rural areas, they think anthrax is a bad disease, and they would be upset if they thought that their children were inoculated. And I said, yes, it is a bad disease, but we are around a lot of sheep and goats in Saudi Arabia. So it would be better to have them inoculated, and hopefully they wouldn't get the disease than not be inoculated and be right there with the animals. So that's what happened. And then, oh, about a month later, the Iraqis were shooting missiles in the area, and my driver and I was driving through an area and there was a lot of dead sheep and goats in that area. So either they had a disease that they died from or else there was gas killed them from the rocket. I don't know. But anyway I thought I'm glad that--{cell phone rings}--I thought I shut that off. Anyway so I was glad that we got inoculated from it.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: I'm curious did--were there any entertainers that came through that--

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: Like Bob Hope and who else were some of the--

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Right

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: Marilyn Monroe, did she--

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Well, in Vietnam Peter--what was his last name--he came, Fonda, Peter Fonda, came out to where we were up in the jungle, and so we, you know, talked to him just a little bit. And then I was flying with this aviator one day and we were looking for enemy, and we got over the radio that there was a VIP, an actress from the Bob Cummings Show that was going to land at our area. Well, you ladies are too young, but Bob Cummings was a TV star that had a show, and he had all these lovely ladies on there. And he had--his secretary was Schultzy, that was her name, Ann Davis, and she wasn't that--she wasn't, you know, the real gorgeous person, but anyway we though, oh, man, he's got--you know, it's a lady. So we took off and went back and landed, and it was Schultzy that came out, but she was nice. She was great.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: Okay. One last question. What was your favorite memory of the whole military experience?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Oh, dear. Well, the whole experience was a good memory really, except seeing people die. But being with people and working with people and finding out that people throughout the world want the same thing we do, they just want to live their life and have a happy life and, you know, and not be scared or afraid or just lead a happy life. That's people throughout the world, and they're--most of them are very friendly. And, oh, another interesting thing was that one day--I worked so close with the Saudi Arabians, and we're setting up these prisoner of war camps that I got word from this Saudi Arabian general that General Khalid, he was a prince, he was like the chief of staff for the military for Saudi Arabia wanted to see me in his office. And, of course, I knew the person by name, and so the Saudi Arabians were all excited that I worked with. And so I went back and told my general, and he said, fine. And I told General Schwarzkopf's staff officer who was a Provost Marshal, military police, and he said, well, I want to send one of my men with you, a lieutenant colonel, and he said that's just as a precaution. So that if the--so that if they want you to make a commitment that it is a commitment that, you know, that we agree with, you know. And that--just to be there as--in case something comes up that maybe wasn't said or was implied that he would be there. So he and I went, and, of course, we waited outside of his office, and he called us in. And he talked to us about setting up prisoner of war camps and what he wanted and all that. So I was--that was one of the highlights of--that I was being called in his office to talk to him. That he wanted to talk to me.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: Is there anything you want to ask sitting here silently through?

sp.speaker: Sheryl G. Weatherford
sp.p: Trying to think. What was the general--the last name Khalid?

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Yeah, Khalid

sp.speaker: Sheryl G. Weatherford
sp.p: K-H--

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Yeah, I can't--I don't remember his name. Prince Khalid, K-H-A-L-I-D, or something like that

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: That's what we'll go with. And then there was a village, Nuc Van.

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Nuc Van, Nuc Van. N-U-C, capital V-A-N or V-A-H-N. One thing about different countries in the world, especially Saudi Arabia, for English they go by a lot by how it sounds. Like there was a sign, I have a picture of it, a sign on the highway saying "Passport Chick." And so--and one thing I learned the numbers. So when I teach math at high school and middle school if I want to write the answers when I go out, you know, work with the students, I can put them on the board in Arabic and that way all I have to do is look up there, and like for number one the answer is 510 or whatever, it is all in Arabic. So...

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: Thank you very much.

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Yes, ma'am.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: This has been very enlightening to me.

sp.speaker: Sheryl G. Weatherford
sp.p: Trying to think of--do you have any experiences with the--like with the heat in Saudi Arabia because I had a--my cousin flew for them--or flew for the Air Force, and he would say--and he was in Desert Storm, and the cockpits would get so hot, you couldn't touch the airplane--you know, you couldn't touch the instruments.

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Well, growing up on a farm in Iowa, it got very hot, and I am used -- in Vietnam I loved the heat. I don't like cool weather, so I would be out there, you know, and it wouldn't bother--other people it would, I had to watch my troops so that they wouldn't become dehydrated. And--but I enjoyed it. I liked being out in the heat. It's a God awful hot. I remember one day on--at home we came in, we were bailing hay, and we came in for lunch. And my dad always had the markets on, and right after the markets was the news, and they said, well, the warden of the local prison in Iowa said it was too hot for the prisoners to go out and work so he's going to let them stay in the air conditioned prison. I looked at my dad, and he said, this isn't the prison. We are going out and bailing hay.

sp.speaker: Sheryl G. Weatherford
sp.p: I can't think of anything else. So we've done the 30 minutes, so we're good on--

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: Oh, yeah, we're good on time.

sp.speaker: Fred See
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Sheryl G. Weatherford
sp.p: Yeah, we're great on time.

sp.speaker: Ann Banta
sp.p: Time-wise is good.
